raw_response:
Six existing mechanisms are useful comparisons for the numeric-sequence and loop-design problem.

1. Haskell 1.3 arithmetic-sequence notation and Prelude-bound translation
URL: https://www.altocumulus.org/haskell-report/exps.html
Haskell's arithmetic-sequence expressions show how compact syntax can express regular numeric indices while translating through specified enumeration bindings instead of an arbitrary locally rebound helper name.
Transfer caveat: the step is the difference between the first two values, the terminal boundary is inclusive, and a zero increment can make an infinite sequence. Enumeration is overloaded through Enum, so fixed helper binding does not by itself justify primitive-integer optimization.
Date evidence: the opened Haskell 1.3 report contains the relevant syntax and translation; the official edition index at https://www.haskell.org/definition/ dates this version to May 1996. The edition index is later corroboration.

2. Common Lisp LOOP arithmetic clauses
URL: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/Groups/AI/html/cltl/clm/node244.html
LOOP's from, below/to, and by clauses make the initial index, stopping boundary, and stride explicit in readable iteration syntax.
Transfer caveat: LOOP is a loop macro, not inherently a first-class sequence, and its grammar would require a deliberate adaptation to Python's bindings and mutation behavior.
Date evidence: the opened second-edition text displays the arithmetic grammar in a March 1989 correction; the book is identified as a 1990 edition in the opened SRFI bibliography.

3. Python 2.0 range and xrange
URL: https://stuff.mit.edu/afs/sipb.mit.edu/project/python/share/doc/lib/built-in-funcs.html
The existing range/xrange pair supplies the exact start/stop/step behavior and contrasts materialized lists with numeric sequences generated on demand.
Transfer caveat: the boundary is exclusive and a zero step is an error. Ordinary function calls preserve both the readability issue and the possibility of rebinding the helper. Any optimization based on the intended built-in must establish that binding or guard it; fixed indices also do not guarantee safe behavior when the sequence changes length.
Date evidence: the opened title page at https://stuff.mit.edu/afs/sipb.mit.edu/project/python/share/doc/lib/lib.html identifies release 2.0 dated October 16, 2000.

4. FORTRAN 77 DO loop control
URL: https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/805-4939/6j4m0vn8c/index.html
FORTRAN DO shows a direct start/limit/increment loop construct with entry-time parameter evaluation and an established iteration count that can guide an explicit numeric-loop design.
Transfer caveat: this is a loop construct rather than a sequence value, its terminal boundary is inclusive, it restricts changes to the loop variable, and overflow requires attention.
Date evidence: unknown for the retrieved manual edition. The official chapter and index were opened, but a website copyright footer does not establish when this edition was published.

5. Scheme R5RS do iteration and hygienic expansion
URL: https://conservatory.scheme.org/schemers/Documents/Standards/R5RS/HTML/r5rs-Z-H-7.html
R5RS do offers an alternative that combines initialization, a stop test, and an update expression, while its hygienic expansion rules illustrate how generated helper references can retain their intended bindings.
Transfer caveat: it is more verbose than range notation, and evaluating tests and steps on each iteration gives different behavior from precomputing a range. Scheme permits local bindings to shadow syntactic keywords, and user-written operators retain their normal binding semantics.
Date evidence: the opened report specifies the relevant iteration and macro rules; its standards archive identifies the report's 1998 publications.

6. SRFI-1 iota and its public reference implementation
Specification: https://srfi.schemers.org/srfi-1/srfi-1.html
Code: https://github.com/scheme-requests-for-implementation/srfi-1/blob/master/srfi-1-reference.scm
iota and its actual public code provide a count/start/step progression generator that can serve as an alternative API and a concrete implementation reference.
Transfer caveat: it accepts a count instead of an end boundary and eagerly constructs a list; conversion from end-based inputs can reintroduce length arithmetic. An ordinary procedure name also does not solve Python's rebinding constraint.
Date evidence: retained as later evidence. The live specification lists final status in 1999 but also revisions through October 2026, and the opened implementation was not pinned to a pre-cutoff revision.

Design implications are inferred from these mechanisms, not claims of measured performance or adoption. A readable design must state whether the end is inclusive, how descending and zero-step cases behave, and whether bounds are evaluated once or repeatedly. Position-based mutation additionally needs explicit behavior for length changes. For optimization, recognizing a helper's spelling alone is insufficient under the rebinding constraint in the problem; specified translation bindings or verified runtime bindings address different parts of that issue.
